newsitem.title: USA: Merrill Lynch aims at smooth succession.
newsitem.headline: Merrill Lynch aims at smooth succession.

text.p: In naming David Komansky its next chief executive and chairman Merrill Lynch & Co completes a two-year process intended to make the transfer of leadership at the nation's largest brokerage as smooth as possible.

Komansky and current chairman and chief executive Daniel Tully said in a joint interview that the basic strategies employed by the nation's largest firm would remain in place after Komansky takes hold of the reins.
Tully, who turns 65 in 1997 will retire as Merrill's chairman on April 15, when the firm holds its annual meeting.

Komansky, 57, has been the obvious choice to replace Tully since he was named Merrill's president and chief executive in January, 1995. He serves as one of three employee directors on Merrill's board and as a member of the firm's office of chairman and office of chief executive.
"Dave has been intimately involved in the decision making process at the highest levels of the firm for at least the last 10 years," said Tully, "not just the two years he was president."
Komansky said Merrill would continue to look inward and outward for growth opportunities.

"As in the past, we examine both growth by acquisition and organic growth," Komanksy said. "I'm sure we'll take advantage of both means going forward as we have in the past. There are tremendous opportunites for us in every corner of the world."
Nor does Komansky plan to change Merrill's approach to litigation brought by Orange County against the firm.
"It doesn't change our position at all," Komansky said. "We've felt all along we've done nothing inappropriate and we will defend that feeling in any way that's at our disposal."

Wall Street accepted the news of Komansky's ascent in stride, with Merrill Lynch shares off 1/8 to 67-5/8. The reception stood in contrast to a week ago, when AT&T Corp shares suffered a steady and sharp decline after its surprise selection of John Walter to succeed Robert Allen.

"It has been long expected that Dave would take over," said Raphael Soifer, analyst at Brown Brothers Harriman. "The intention was to make this a very seamless transition and this is situation normal."
